idiom_name: caller-owned buffer struct + append function (or an open_memstream FILE* sink)
implementation_notes: C has no generic container, so the collecting parameter is a hand-written sink: a growable struct with an append entry point (`sb_add`, `sb_addf`) passed by pointer to every producer. stdio provides the same shape for text through `FILE *` and `open_memstream(&buf, &len)` (the buffer grows as the stream is written), and GLib's `GString` with `g_string_append`/`g_string_append_printf` is the dominant library version. What replaces the classic structure: the collector class collapses into the struct plus its append API while the caller keeps ownership and cleanup; the full struct-plus-append form stays justified whenever appends must be ordered and the buffer reused across a parse or render walk.
pitfalls: Pass the buffer by pointer: a struct copy silently collects into a temporary and the caller sees an empty result.
Every append may `realloc` and move the storage, so never keep a `char *` into the buffer across calls to the append function - that stale pointer is the classic C version of this pattern's bug.
Check allocation failure (and `open_memstream` returning NULL) inside the append path, or a failed grow turn into silent truncation or undefined behaviour.
